facts.statement: Haplocheirus lived during the Late Jurassic, between 161.2 and 158.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic~161.2 to 158.7 Ma -

facts.statement: The genus Haplocheirus was described by Choiniere and colleagues in 2010.
facts.quote: authority: Choiniere et al., 2010

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Haplocheirus sollers.
facts.quote: type_species: Haplocheirus sollers

facts.statement: Haplocheirus is generally classified as an alvarezsauroid, though some researchers question this assignment.
facts.quote: It is generally considered to be an alvarezsauroid, although some researchers have questioned this assignment.

facts.statement: The genus Haplocheirus contains only one species, H. sollers, known from a mostly complete skeleton that includes the skull.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, H. sollers, which is known from a mostly complete skeleton including the skull.

facts.statement: The single known specimen of Haplocheirus is preserved in near-perfect three-dimensional detail.
facts.quote: The quality of the preservation in the only known specimen of Haplocheirus is near-perfect and preserves the animal in three dimensions.

facts.statement: The type and only specimen of Haplocheirus is designated IVPP V15988.
facts.quote: The type and only specimen of Haplocheirus was given the designation IVPP V15988.

facts.statement: Dating of volcanic feldspar places the habitat of Haplocheirus at the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: 40Ar/39Ar dating of volcanic feldspar at this locality places it at the span between the Callovian and Oxfordian boundary, and Haplocheirus was discovered in the upper part of this unit, which is interpreted as being Oxfordian in age.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus was discovered in fine-grained red or brown mudstone.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus was discovered in a more traditional fine-grained red or brown mudstone.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Haplocheirus was found with articulated remains of a crocodyliform.
facts.quote: Subsequent publications have noted that the holotype was also discovered with the articulated remains of a crocodyliform.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus was formally described in the journal Science in 2010 by Choiniere, Xu, Clark, Forster, Guo, and Han.
facts.quote: The formal description of Haplocheirus was published in 2010 in the journal Science by Jonah Choiniere, Xu Xing, James M. Clark, Catherine A. Forster, Yu Guo, and Fenglu Han.

facts.statement: The genus name Haplocheirus comes from the Greek words for "simple" and "hand".
facts.quote: Their explanation of the etymology is that the genus name comes from the Greek words "haplo", meaning "simple", and "cheirus", meaning "hand".

facts.statement: The species name sollers is derived from the Latin word for "skillful".
facts.quote: The specific epithet, H. sollers is derived from the Latin word for "skillful".

facts.statement: An amended diagnosis and detailed skull monograph for Haplocheirus were published in 2014 by many of the original authors.
facts.quote: An amended diagnosis was published by many of the same authors in 2014 along with a detailed osteological monograph about the specimen's skull.

facts.statement: Before Haplocheirus was found, there was a debate over whether alvarezsauroids were closely related to birds or if their similarities were due to convergent evolution.
facts.quote: Prior to the discovery of Haplocheirus, the phylogenetic placement of alvarezsauroids was uncertain. Some authors believed them to be the sister group to avialae, while others believed the anatomical similarity to birds were the result of convergent evolution.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus suggests that alvarezsauroid ancestry was conventional and not closely related to birds like dromaeosaurs or troodontids.
facts.quote: The similarities between Haplocheirus and other primitive maniraptorans provided evidence that their ancestry was much more conventional and that they were not very closely related to birds, compared to dromaeosaurs and troodontids.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus was a small coelurosaur but one of the largest alvarezsaurs.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus was a relatively small coelurosaur, but it was one of the largest alvarezsaurs.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Haplocheirus was about 2 meters long and weighed 21 kilograms.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estimated that it was about 2 m long and weighed about 21 kg.

facts.statement: Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated Haplocheirus was about 60 centimeters tall at the hip.
facts.quote: Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi gave a similar size estimate to Paul and additionally estimate that it would have been about 60 cm tall at the hip.

facts.statement: Later research suggests the holotype was a juvenile, with adult Haplocheirus estimated to weigh around 41 kilograms.
facts.quote: Later authors have noted that the holotype is most-likely a juvenile individual, and Zichuan Qin and colleagues estimated that an adult Haplocheirus could have weighed around 41 kg.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus was identified as an alvarezsaur based on several unambiguous shared traits with that group.
facts.quote: It was identified as an alvarezsaur in its original description due to the presence of several unambiguous alvarezsauroid synapomorphies.

facts.statement: Key alvarezsaur traits in Haplocheirus include a long pterygoid process, inclined basisphenoid, large humeral tuberosity, large ectepicondyle, a furrow on the second finger phalanx, and a conical femoral lateral condyle.
facts.quote: These included: a long process on the pterygoid bone, a vertically inclined basisphenoid, a large tuberosity within the humerus, a large ectepicondyle on the humerus, a furrow on the surface of the first phalanx of the second finger, and a conical shape to the lateral condyle of the femur.

facts.statement: A suggested unique trait, a second mandibular fenestra, is believed to be an artifact of fossilization rather than a biological feature.
facts.quote: One of the suggested autapomorphies — a second mandibular fenestra — is believed to have been taphonomic in origin.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus differs from derived alvarezsaurids by having heterodont dentition.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus is different from derived alvarezsaurids in the presence of heterodont dentition.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus had circular premaxillary teeth without serrations and flattened maxillary teeth with serrations along some of their length.
facts.quote: The premaxillary teeth are circular in cross-section and lack serrations whereas the maxillary teeth are mediolaterally flattened and have serrations along some of their length.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus had four premaxillary teeth, at least 30 maxillary teeth, and 30 to 40 dentary teeth.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus possessed four premaxillarly teeth, like most theropods; and at least 30 maxillary teeth and between 30-40 dentary teeth, although some of the alveoli are obscured by the matrix.

facts.statement: Very few theropods have such high tooth counts, with only Pelecanimimus, Shuvuuia, Falcarius, and Byronosaurus approaching this total.
facts.quote: Very few theropods have tooth counts this high, with the only taxa approaching this total being Pelecanimimus, Shuvuuia, Falcarius, and Byronosaurus.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus resembles basal theropods like Ornitholestes, Pelecanimimus, and Nqwebasaurus in having a triradiate jugal bone, complete postorbital bar, and a quadrate ascending ramus contacting the squamosal.
facts.quote: It is much more similar to basal members of theropod clades like Ornitholestes, Pelecanimimus, and Nqwebasaurus in the presence of a triradiate jugal bone, a complete postorbital bar, and an ascending ramus of the quadrate which contacts the squamosal.

facts.statement: Some authors argue that Haplocheirus may be more closely related to ornithomimosaurs or that its classification as an alvarezsaur is not robust.
facts.quote: However, some authors believe that these traits indicate closer affinities with ornithomimosaurs or at least that the placement of Haplocheirus as an alvarezsauroid is not very robust.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus retained the ancestral saurischian pubic bone orientation, differing from later alvarezsaurs which evolved an ornithischian-like pubic condition.
facts.quote: It also preserves the ancestral saurischian pubic condition, unlike derived alvarezsaurs, which have the ornithischian pubic condition.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus possessed a notably robust first finger that was stronger than its second and third fingers.
facts.quote: One of the most unique aspects of the postcranial anatomy Haplocheirus is the robust first finger in comparison to the other two fingers.

facts.statement: The second and third metacarpals of Haplocheirus were narrowing, a trait seen as a precursor to the bone fusion found in later species like Patagonykus.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus also demonstrates a trend towards narrowing the second and third metacarpals, which is believed to be a precondition for the full coossification of these bones in animals like Patagonykus.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus exhibits a transitional semi-lunate carpal structure, showing an intermediate stage in the evolution of wrist bones typical of derived maniraptorans.
facts.quote: Another notable feature of Haplocheirus is that it preserves a transitional state in the formation of the semi-lunate carpal, which characterizes most derived maniraptorans.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses by Choiniere and colleagues identified Haplocheirus as the most basal member of the alvarezsauroidea group.
facts.quote: They recovered Haplocheirus as the most basal member of alvarezsauroidea.

facts.statement: While some analyses place Haplocheirus near ornithomimosaurs, researchers note that support for this relationship is stronger than previous hypotheses linking it to avialae.
facts.quote: However, they do remark that an affinity with ornithomimosaurs is much more strongly supported than the former hypothesis.

facts.statement: Scott Hartman and colleagues proposed an alternative classification placing Haplocheirus within the compsognathids, though they published only an abbreviated version of their phylogenetic tree.
facts.quote: In this analysis, they recovered Haplocheirus as a compsognathid, however they only published an abbreviated topology in their final publication which did not include detailed trees of the various stem-maniraptoran groups like compsognathidae.

facts.statement: Unlike most alvarezsaurs with highly modified forelimbs, Haplocheirus appears to have used its hands with proficiency comparable to other theropods of similar arm proportions.
facts.quote: Haplocheirus seems to have been able to use its hands as proficiently as other theropods with similarly proportioned arms and hands.

facts.statement: Histological examination revealed four lines of arrested growth, indicating the single known specimen of Haplocheirus was approximately four years old at death.
facts.quote: They identified four distinct lines of arrested growth (or LAGs), which strongly implies that the individual was four-years-old when it died.

facts.statement: Based on growth curves derived from related species, researchers estimate the adult mass of Haplocheirus to be between 38 kg and 43 kg.
facts.quote: They give a range of between 38 kg and 43 kg for an adult individual.

facts.statement: Large eye orbits and wide scleral apertures suggest that Haplocheirus may have been adapted for nocturnal activity.
facts.quote: In their findings, they suggested that the large orbits and wide scleral aperture suggest that Haplocheirus and its relative Shuvuuia were adapted for nocturnality.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus possessed unusually long cochlear canals compared to other non-avian theropods, an adaptation likely linked to enhanced hearing capabilities.
facts.quote: They also remarked that the cochlear canals of Haplocheirus and its relatives were proportionally longer than those of other theropods, which is an adaptation believed to correlate with improved hearing capabilities, and one which is very uncommon in non-avian theropods.

facts.statement: The slender teeth and lightweight skull of Haplocheirus suggest it primarily fed on small vertebrates.
facts.quote: These traits suggest that Haplocheirus primarily fed on small vertebrates.

facts.statement: Some researchers hypothesize that the robust first finger of Haplocheirus was an adaptation for digging into tree trunks to access insects, similar to the modern aye-aye.
facts.quote: Some authors have also suggested that the increase in the robustness of the first finger may have been an adaptation for digging in tree trunks for insects, similar to the modern aye-aye.

facts.statement: Other authors argue that the first finger of Haplocheirus was not ecologically unique and that its diet was similar to that of other similarly sized theropods.
facts.quote: However, other authors have suggested that it was unremarkable in its ecology and likely had a diet very similar to most similarly sized theropods.

facts.statement: The only known remains of Haplocheirus were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.
facts.quote: The only remains of Haplocheirus so far described were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.

facts.statement: Haplocheirus lived during the interval from 164 to 159 million years ago, spanning the transition from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: This locality is a part of the lower member of the Shishugou Formation, which ranges from 164 to 159 million years ago.

facts.statement: The Late Jurassic climate in the Haplocheirus habitat was temperate with seasonal patterns of wet and dry periods.
facts.quote: The climate of the area during the Late Jurassic was temperate and seasonally wet and dry.
